newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian PM to start coalition talks this week.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian PM to start coalition talks this week.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek, whose Liberal Democrats won most votes in a general election two weeks ago, will start talks with other parties this week to form a government, a party spokeswoman said on Monday.
"We expect all parties to accept Drnovsek's invitation for talks which should start by the end of this week," spokeswoman Petra Skofic told Reuters.

But Drnovsek, who has served as prime minister for four of Slovenia's five years of independence from Yugoslavia in 1991, could have a battle on his hands returning to power as premier, political analysts said.

His centre-left Liberal Democrats won 25 of the 90 seats in parliament in the November 10 general election, but face a rightwing alliance of three parties which together hold 45 seats, one short of an absolute majority.
The so-called "Slovenian Spring" alliance, comprises the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats, who want to unseat Drnovsek.

The alliance is pushing for Marjan Podobnik, 35-year-old leader of the People's Party, to be candidate for prime minister. His pro-farmer party won 19 seats, the biggest share of deputies among the three rightwing parties.
"Our leader will meet Drnovsek presumably this week, but we shall insist that Podobnik gets the mandate to form the next government," People's Party spokesman Jaka Sever said.

The "Spring" alliance appeared to be in a better position to form the next government, analysts said, but they cast doubt on claims by the right that it had secured the support of a deputy from a smaller party, giving them the vital 46th seat to allow them to rule.
"I do not believe they have the extra seat, but their chances of forming the new government are slightly better than those of Drnovsek," political analyst Miha Kovac said.
President Milan Kucan has to name a candidate for premier within 30 days of the first session of the new parliament, set for November 28.

The formation of a rightwing government could slow down Slovenia's bid to join the European Union, which Drnovsek had targeted for 2001. While all three parties back EU entry, the People's Party has stressed that it would insist on special protection for the Alpine country's farmers.
The already sluggish privatisation process may also become bogged down as the right has indicated it may reconsider privatisations completed under Drnovsek's government.
All political parties, except the United List of Social Democrats, the former communists, support NATO membership.
Slovenia has the highest gross domestic product (GDP) per capita among Europe's ex-communist states with $9,352 in 1995.
